planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a fast-draining succulent/cactus mix; this Bredasdorp-area species rarely offsets, so most propagation is from rooted divisions or seed.

directions: Native to the Bredasdorp and Cape Agulhas area of South Africa's Western Cape, this stemless rosette bears thick, blunt, turban-shaped leaves whose flattened tips carry pale, striated windows that let light reach the photosynthetic tissue below. Grow in bright indirect light in a mineral-rich, fast-draining mix, since the leaf faces can scorch under unfiltered midday sun yet lose their translucent patterning in deep shade. It closely resembles Haworthia retusa but stays more compact and offsets only sparingly in cultivation, so division should wait until pups have rooted on their own. Water deeply only once the mix has dried out completely, and withhold water almost entirely through the winter rest.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a fast-draining succulent/cactus mix; a Mossel Bay endemic whose rough-textured leaf forms are especially prized by collectors.

directions: Endemic to a narrow strip of the Mossel Bay district in South Africa's Western Cape, this diminutive stemless rosette carries flat, grey-green leaves with rounded rather than pointed tips, and many wild and cultivated forms develop a rough, papillate surface studded with tiny raised bumps instead of a smooth window. Site it in bright indirect light in a gritty succulent mix, since strong direct sun can bronze or scorch the flattened leaf faces while low light causes stretching and loss of the tight rosette form. It is frequently confused with Haworthia retusa, H. bayeri, and H. magnifica, but its rounded leaf tips and characteristically rough or spotted texture set it apart. Water only after the mix is completely dry, and reduce watering further during the cooler dormant months.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in an especially fast-draining succulent/cactus mix; this rare, restricted-range species is usually propagated from leaf cuttings or seed rather than offsets.

directions: Restricted to a small area of the Eastern Cape near the Springbokvlakte, this solitary rosette produces some of the largest, most swollen leaf windows in the genus, with plump, rounded tips that bulge visibly above the soil line. Because wild populations are so localized and slow-growing, and the plant rarely forms offsets, most cultivated specimens are raised from leaf cuttings or seed rather than divisions. Keep it in bright indirect light in an especially fast-draining, mineral-rich mix, since the inflated leaf faces are prone to splitting or rot if overwatered or kept in stagnant, humid air. Allow the mix to dry out completely between waterings, and water only sparingly during the winter rest.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a fast-draining succulent/cactus mix; once treated as a variety of Haworthia arachnoidea, now recognized as its own species.

directions: Occurring across the Nama Karoo and Succulent Karoo regions of South Africa's Eastern and Western Cape, this species forms a compact rosette of narrow, fibrous-edged leaves lined with soft, hair-like bristles reminiscent of a spiderweb. Once classified as a variety of Haworthia arachnoidea, it is now recognized as a distinct species, separated by subtler differences in leaf proportion and bristle density that specialists use to tell the two apart. Grow in bright indirect light in a coarse, fast-draining mix, since the fine bristled margins can trap excess moisture against the leaf base and invite rot if the plant is kept too wet or too shaded. Let the soil dry completely between waterings, and divide offset clumps once new rosettes have formed their own roots.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a fast-draining succulent/cactus mix; one of the earliest Haworthia species formally described, dating to the 18th century.

directions: One of the earliest Haworthia species formally described, this Cape Province native forms a low rosette of soft, yellow-green leaves edged with small, fine spines. As the rosette matures, the foliage deepens to a darker green while raised white tubercles emerge across the leaf surface, giving older plants a noticeably spotted, textured look quite different from the smooth-windowed retuse species. Provide bright indirect light in a well-drained succulent mix; too little light causes the rosette to stretch and lose its compact form, while harsh direct sun can bleach or scar the developing spots. It flowers readily from a slender stalk, producing pale off-white blooms in spring, and clumps can be propagated by dividing rooted offsets.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, filtered light in a fast-draining succulent/cactus mix, echoing the sheltered, shrub-shaded sites it favors in the wild.

directions: Ranging along the Swartberg foothills of South Africa's Western and Eastern Cape, this species earns its name — decipiens, 'deceptive' — from how easily it is confused with the closely related Haworthia arachnoidea, though its leaves run shorter, flatter, and paler, with translucent tips and coarser, more widely spaced marginal bristles. In the wild it typically grows tucked beneath the shelter of low shrubs, so in cultivation it does best in bright but filtered light rather than harsh, exposed sun, in a gritty and fast-draining mix. The rosette contracts and tightens during drought, then plumps back up quickly once watered, so it should be allowed to dry out fully between thorough waterings. Propagate by separating rooted offsets from the base of established clumps.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a fast-draining succulent/cactus mix; a reliable, longer-season bloomer among collector Haworthias.

directions: Native to South Africa's Cape Province, this species forms a rosette of dark green, lance-shaped leaves that curve and twist outward rather than lying flat, giving established clumps a slightly tousled, sculptural look; a form known as var. dentata adds small marginal teeth along the leaf edges. Grow in bright indirect light in a coarse, fast-draining succulent mix, since the darker foliage can scorch under intense direct sun but loses its rich color and firm form in low light. True to its name, it sends up flowering stalks more readily and over a longer season than many of its relatives, making it one of the more reliable bloomers among collector Haworthias. Water thoroughly only once the mix has dried out completely, and propagate by dividing rooted offsets from the base.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright light with some gentle direct sun in a fast-draining succulent/cactus mix; tougher and more sun-tolerant than the soft window-leaved Haworthia species.

directions: Found in the Little Karoo region of South Africa's Western and Eastern Cape, this species produces stiff, upright leaves arranged in tidy vertical ranks that often twist into a gentle spiral as the rosette matures. The typical form has a dark, harshly textured surface covered in dense raised tubercles that feel like sandpaper to the touch, though several named varieties range from smooth and pale to sparsely studded with just a few large bumps. Grow in bright light with some gentle direct morning sun, which this tougher, rough-leaved Haworthiopsis tolerates far better than the soft, window-leaved Haworthia species, in a coarse mineral mix that drains quickly. Water deeply and let the soil dry fully between waterings, and divide rooted offsets to propagate.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a very fast-draining succulent/cactus mix; water sparingly and let the plant complete its natural dry-season dieback rather than forcing continuous growth.

directions: Native to the Cape Provinces of South Africa, this small rosette is best known for its dramatic dry-season survival strategy: as the ground dries out, its outer leaves wither into thin, papery, brownish sheaths that wrap tightly around the crown, making the plant look all but dead until rain returns. Beneath that dried covering, a tight cluster of leaf tips carries small, nearly colorless translucent windows that keep photosynthesizing even while the rest of the rosette is dormant. Once watered, the papery sheaths rehydrate and the leaves plump back up to a pale green within days, so growers should resist the urge to keep watering a shriveled-looking specimen out of season. Keep it in bright indirect light in a very fast-draining mineral mix, and water sparingly, allowing the plant to complete its natural dry-down cycle each year.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a fast-draining succulent/cactus mix; offsets freely, so clumps are easy to divide for propagation.

directions: Endemic to the Little Karoo between Barrydale and Oudtshoorn in South Africa's Western Cape, this species forms tight, offsetting clumps of soft, pale green, lance-shaped leaves whose keel and margins carry a narrow band of translucency rather than a broad window across the leaf face. In habitat it hybridizes naturally with Haworthia arachnoidea, and cultivated plants can show intermediate bristle and color traits depending on their origin. Grow in bright indirect light in a gritty, fast-draining mix, since the soft pale foliage is more prone to sunburn than tougher Haworthiopsis species but will fade and stretch in deep shade. It offsets readily to form dense clumps, making division of rooted pups the easiest way to propagate.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
